item.title: Wraith: Unwrapping the Bytecode VM Inside a 2 KB wasm Module
item.description: A 2 KB WebAssembly file with one exported function and two imports. No strings, no symbols, nothing readable. Inside it hides a tiny bytecode VM that checks the flag one byte at a time, and every check inverts in closed form.

item.title: Fianchetto: A 2048-Bit Modulus, Undone by a 160-Bit Secret
item.description: The public modulus is a healthy 2048 bits. The public exponent is 2045 bits, which is the tell: when e is nearly as large as N, the private exponent d must be tiny. Wiener's attack walks the continued fraction of e/N until the key falls out.

item.title: DeadBolt: Two Signatures, One Nonce, One Dead Key
item.description: A release-signing service on secp256k1 published two ECDSA signatures that share the same r. That one repeated value is the whole challenge: the nonce falls out of it, and the nonce hands you the private key. No lattice, no brute force, just modular arithmetic.

item.title: Pearl Harbour: A Forged Captain and a Capability That Sailed to Root
item.description: A tiny Flask app called the Pacific Fleet Cargo and Manifest Registry. It hands out guest JWTs, trusts the kid and alg fields in the header, and shells out to pdftotext with a filename I control. Three mistakes later: root.

item.title: Phantom Drop: A PowerShell Dropper Wearing a Windows Update Badge
item.description: A 45-packet capture, 52 seconds long, that shows a Windows implant checking in, pulling a payload, staging it, and mailing credentials home. Almost all of it is plain HTTP, and the flag is sitting in the exfil report.

item.title: Dead Reckoning: When the Paperwork Lies, Trust the Physics
item.description: A corrupted flight data recorder log, 13 ghost entries, and four different pieces of paperwork all trying to send me to the wrong answer. Reconstructing a Cessna's true flight path with nothing but dead-reckoning physics.

item.title: Nexus: When Every Field Lies, Trust the Scorer
item.description: A custom hash chain, 8 data blocks, a 32-byte initial state, and every labeled field in the binary pointing somewhere wrong. Plus a hash chain that turns out not to exist. Reversing the only field that tells the truth: the official scorer itself.

item.title: The Last Day: HR Said It Was Routine. The Logs Disagreed.
item.description: An insider threat hidden inside hand-crafted Windows event logs, records Event Viewer physically cannot show. The after-hours logon, the staged files, the 7-Zip exfil, and the flag buried in HR's own paperwork.

item.title: AfricaHackon: Rooted or Not? Bypassing a Root Check Without Rooting Anything
item.description: Android APK reversing, XOR key recovered, static analysis only. A vault app gates its debug panel behind a root check, but the flag is computed statically. No rooting, no emulator, no Frida needed.

item.title: Packet Whisperer: The One Where DNS Snitched on Itself
item.description: DNS exfiltration reversed from a PCAP, pure Python, zero Wireshark. A complete walkthrough of how attackers smuggle data out via DNS TXT queries and how to catch them.

item.title: HackTheBox: SecretCorp Writeup
item.description:
🧩 Challenge Overview

This challenge involved exploiting a misconfigured web app to gain unauthorized access to internal data.

🔍 Enumeration

```bash nmap -sC -sV 10.10.10.10 ``` Discovered ports:

  • 80/tcp, HTTP (Apache 2.4.41)
  • 22/tcp, SSH (OpenSSH 8.2p1)

💥 Exploitation

During directory fuzzing with `ffuf`, found `/backup.zip`. Unzipped credentials for `admin:SuperSecure123`. Login exposed an LFI vulnerability at `index.php?file=…`.

```bash curl “http://target/index.php?file=../../../../etc/passwd” ```

🧑‍💻 Privilege Escalation

After gaining shell access: ```bash linpeas.sh | tee output.txt ``` Found `/usr/local/bin/backup` with SUID bit. Exploited it via `bash -p` to spawn a root shell.
